newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq's dinar still shaky despite state measures.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's dinar still shaky despite state measures.

text.p: Intervention by Iraq's Central Bank last week has achieved relative success in stabilising its volatile currency but has failed to nudge it any higher, traders and money changers in Baghdad said on Sunday.
They said last week's measures taken by the government allowing state banks to sell hard currency in exchange for the dinar for the first time had only saved the dinar from a further slump.
"They (the state banks) have not been able to boost the value of the dinar because the amount of dollars they sell to people is small, not exceeding $500 a day," one trader said.
He said: "Also the exchange price of the dollar to the dinar set by the banks is more or less equal to that of the spot market."
The rate set by official banks on Sunday morning was 1,535 dinars to one dollar while the spot market was 1,550.
"The exchange rate (of banks) is not firm. It changes every day in accordance with the (spot) market," a bank official told Reuters.

State banks were authorised by the Iraqi Central Bank to sell hard currency on Tuesday. When the decision was first implemented on Wednesday morning the dinar surged to 1,370 against the dollar up from 1,555 prior to its application.

"A committee was set up at the Central Bank which meets every morning and decides the rate. It would be less than that of the commercial markets," said Zuhair Kassab, Deputy Director-General of al-Rasheed, one of the only two governmental banks in Iraq.
Earlier this year, the government allowed several private companies to sell and buy hard currencies with rates close to that of the spot market.
One money changer, who is an owner of a government-licensed private exchange company, said that the banks had been selling them $1,500 to $2,000 according to the official daily rate.
In the past, kerb dealers and traders in the exchange business risked harsh penalties ranging from long imprisonment to amputations.

The government's decision allowing the sale of hard currency came following a severe slump in the value of the dinar as a result of last month's standoff with Washington over Iraq's backing of one Kurdish group against its rivals.

The dinar's fall was also caused by the delay in implementing a U.N. food-for-oil deal allowing Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicines for its population suffering from nearly six years of U.N. trade sanctions imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
